chapters.name: Impulse Buying
chapters.outfit: an orange hoodie and white sneakers
chapters.icon: a shopping bag with a lightning bolt
sentences: Impulse buying.
Impulse buying is making an unplanned purchase because the excitement of a deal takes over.
You walk into the store for toothpaste, already knowing exactly what you need.
You spot a candle under a red sale sign near the checkout.
You breathe in the candle's sugary vanilla smell.
You skip comparing prices because the offer ends tonight.
You picture the money saved instead of the money leaving your account.
You put the candle beside the toothpaste, proud of your expensive little bargain.
People say buying on sale means saving money.
But a discount still costs you money when you never planned to buy the item.
Over time, those little extras swallow money you needed for the rest of the month.
Your cupboards fill with things you never needed in the first place.
A bargain is still a bill.

chapters.name: Credit Card Minimums
chapters.outfit: a red polo shirt and dark trousers
chapters.icon: a credit card beside one tiny coin
sentences: Credit card minimums.
Credit card minimums are small required payments that keep your account current without clearing most of what you owe.
You tap the smallest payment amount on your banking app.
You breathe easier when the green confirmation checkmark appears on your screen.
You close the app with most of the balance still sitting there.
You find another interest charge on your next statement, despite making no new purchases.
You barely notice the balance move after your next minimum payment.
You start treating that payment like rent for money you already spent.
People think paying the minimum means their debt is under control.
But staying current is not the same as paying it off quickly.
Over time, a slower payoff leaves you paying more interest on the same debt.
Without new charges, paying more than the minimum clears interest-bearing debt faster.
The minimum buys time, not freedom.

chapters.name: Unused Subscriptions
chapters.icon: a dusty television with a price tag
sentences: Unused subscriptions.
Unused subscriptions are paid plans you stopped using that automatically renew until you cancel.
You sign up for a streaming service to watch a show everyone keeps talking about.
You finish the last episode and never open the app again.
You delete it while clearing space for photos on your phone.
You still see its name on your bank statement every month.
You scroll past the charge because it looks too small to matter.
You forget another subscription until its annual renewal receipt lands in your inbox.
People think deleting the app ends the payments.
But removing an icon is not the same as canceling a subscription.
Over time, small charges stack into a substantial expense for services you never touch.
That leaves less money for things you actually need and use.
The app is gone, but the meter is still running.

chapters.name: Late Payments
chapters.outfit: a rumpled white shirt and loose blue tie
sentences: Late payments.
Late payments mean paying a bill after its deadline, with many lenders and service providers adding a fee for the delay.
You see the bill notification while standing in the grocery line.
You swipe it away because your hands are full of bags.
You remember it when a fresh notice shows up with a late fee.
You pay more for the same phone service you already used.
You trust automatic payments to handle the next bill without another thought.
You miss another payment when the linked account runs short of money.
You set a reminder to check whether the payment actually went through.
People say automatic payments mean you never need to think about bills again.
But scheduling a payment is not the same as successfully paying a bill.
Over time, credit payments that stay overdue long enough can damage your credit history.
Forgetfulness has a checkout fee.

chapters.name: Brand Loyalty
chapters.outfit: a black hoodie with an oversized gold logo
chapters.icon: a price tag wearing a crown
sentences: Brand loyalty.
Brand loyalty is choosing the same name automatically because a familiar logo feels like proof of quality.
You grab the bright cereal box before reading the price tag.
You leave the plain store-brand bag sitting untouched on the shelf.
You trust the smiling mascot more than the ingredient list.
You buy the detergent your family used, drawn to its familiar blue bottle.
You walk past a cheaper bottle without comparing what is inside.
You do the same with headphones, letting the logo stand in for checking features.
People believe a familiar brand name guarantees a better product.
But a brand name alone does not prove better durability or performance.
Products with matching features still come with different price tags.
Over time, you keep paying extra without checking what the extra money actually buys.
Your budget shrinks while your shopping choices stay on autopilot.
The logo gets a tip.

chapters.name: Buying Too Cheap
chapters.outfit: a faded blue T-shirt and patched jeans
chapters.icon: a shoe with a detached sole
sentences: Buying too cheap.
Buying too cheap means choosing the lowest price while ignoring how often you will pay to replace it.
You grab the cheapest shoes because the price feels like a small personal victory.
You wear them until the soles peel away and rain seeps into your socks.
You buy another pair because replacing them still looks cheaper than buying something sturdier.
You pay again when the same weak stitching splits beside your little toe.
You stack fresh receipts beside shoes that barely survived a season of walking.
You count the purchase price instead of the days of wear your money actually bought.
People say the cheapest option always saves money.
But savings depend on how long it lasts, not just what it costs upfront.
Paying more does not guarantee better quality or longer life.
Over time, repeated replacements turn the low price into a much bigger yearly bill.
The discount comes with repeat billing.

chapters.name: Skipping Maintenance
chapters.outfit: green mechanic overalls and work boots
chapters.icon: a bicycle wheel with a rusty chain
sentences: Skipping maintenance.
Skipping maintenance means delaying routine care until a cheap fix becomes expensive damage.
You hear a steady drip behind the cupboard door every evening.
You tuck a bowl beneath the pipe instead of fixing the leak.
You empty it each morning like the plumbing has become a pet.
You ignore the damp smell creeping out whenever you open the door.
You feel the cabinet floor give beneath your thumb when you press it.
You finally call for help when the swollen door stops closing.
You get a repair bill that includes the wood beneath the leak.
People think maintenance is wasted money when something still works.
But working and slowly falling apart can happen at the same time.
Over time, neglected problems damage parts that were perfectly fine before.
The money you saved gets swallowed by a much bigger repair.
Neglect charges interest in rotten wood.

chapters.name: Chasing Rewards
chapters.outfit: a hot-pink varsity jacket with star patches
chapters.icon: a rewards card with a gold star
sentences: Chasing rewards.
Chasing rewards means buying things you would have skipped just to earn cashback, points, or other perks.
You spot a bonus offer above the laundry detergent in your shopping app.
You add a scented candle to push your cart past the spending threshold.
You unwrap a vanilla candle you never wanted from a box full of packing paper.
You admire the cashback notification like it arrived without a matching charge.
You watch interest charges swallow the reward when you leave your card balance unpaid.
You finally try redeeming your points and find restrictions blocking the thing you actually wanted.
People call rewards free money.
But cashback returns only a fraction of the extra money you spent.
Over time, chasing the next bonus makes unnecessary spending feel like smart shopping.
Your account gets smaller while your points balance looks impressive.
The trophy is a receipt.

chapters.name: Ignoring Employer Match
chapters.outfit: a navy work uniform with a name badge
chapters.icon: two coins joined by a plus sign
sentences: Ignoring employer match.
Ignoring employer match means missing extra retirement money your employer offers when you contribute to its retirement plan.
You click past the retirement enrollment screen with sandwich crumbs on your keyboard.
You stare at the take-home amount on your first pay stub.
You decide that keeping your paycheck bigger matters more than collecting the match.
You eventually set your contribution below the amount needed to receive the full match.
You leave part of your employer's available contribution sitting unused.
You skip the vesting rules explaining what employer money you keep if you leave.
People say contributing just makes their paycheck smaller.
But when your employer matches contributions, it also puts extra money into your retirement account.
Over time, you keep leaving part of your available retirement money unclaimed.
Your retirement savings are smaller because you never collected all the available help.
You turned a benefit into a brochure.

chapters.name: No Emergency Fund
chapters.outfit: a yellow raincoat and rubber boots
sentences: No emergency fund.
No emergency fund means having no cash buffer between an unexpected expense and borrowing to cover it.
You turn the car key and hear a click instead of an engine.
You stare at the repair quote with payday still out of reach.
You open your banking app and find grocery money, not repair money.
You put the repair on a credit card because you need the car running.
You drive away with a working car and a new monthly payment.
You pay interest on a problem the mechanic has already fixed.
People say emergency savings are wasted money because they just sit there.
But sitting there is the job: cash waits so you do not have to borrow.
Over time, those payments eat the money you need for the next unexpected bill.
You start meeting each new problem with debt left over from the last one.
Your broken car should not come with a subscription.

chapters.name: Waiting to Invest
chapters.outfit: a mint-green sweatshirt with a seedling emblem
chapters.icon: an hourglass beside a small sprout
sentences: Waiting to invest.
Waiting to invest means putting off long-term investing until you feel rich, giving your money less time to grow.
You have your bills paid and emergency savings tucked safely away.
You keep next month's rent out of the market because investments can lose value.
You open an investing app and stare at the amount you could spare.
You decide that little number is not worth the effort.
You close the app and promise to start after your next raise.
You get the raise and find a new reason to wait.
People say investing only matters when you have serious money.
But smaller amounts can still benefit from years of potential growth.
Over time, reinvested returns can earn returns of their own.
Starting later leaves fewer years for that potential growth to build on itself.
Someday is an expensive starting date.

chapters.name: Lifestyle Creep
chapters.outfit: a flashy turquoise tracksuit and gold-colored watch
chapters.icon: a shopping cart with an upward arrow
sentences: Lifestyle creep.
Lifestyle creep happens when your spending rises with your income, swallowing the extra money before you save it.
You celebrate your raise by signing a lease on a car that smells like fresh leather.
You move into a bigger apartment, where your old couch looks like sidewalk furniture.
You replace your usual coffee with a daily order that takes longer to say than to drink.
You add subscriptions because each monthly charge feels small next to your new paycheck.
You open your banking app and find the same thin balance wearing a more expensive outfit.
You consider cutting back, but the car lease makes getting out another expense.
People think a bigger paycheck automatically means more money saved.
But a raise only increases savings when some of that extra income stays unspent.
Over time, the new car smell disappears, but the higher payments keep arriving.
Your upgraded life becomes the minimum you expect to afford.
Your raise hired more bills.
